summary: A 1970 note on protocols and data formats from two RAND authors. It updates RFC 66, was updated by RFC 93, and was replaced by RFC 123.

plainLanguage.summary: A note on agreeing how data is arranged between computers. A newer note replaced it.

questions: what is the initial connection protocol
subtitle: A 1970 RAND note that restates one early connection set-up sequence and argues for adapting programs to the network instead of the reverse.

tldr.problem: Early network users disagreed about how two hosts should set up their first connection, and many existing programs and terminals did not speak the formats other hosts expected.
tldr.mechanism: The note restates the Initial Connection Protocol of RFC 66, proposes a variant that saves two network messages, and describes two adaptable tools: a Form Machine for data formats and a Protocol Manager for command sequences.
tldr.outcome: It is a discussion note, not a standard. It updates RFC 66, was itself updated by RFC 93, and was replaced by RFC 123.

today: This note updates RFC 66, was updated by RFC 93, and was replaced by RFC 123. It is a historical discussion document from December 1970.

sections.title: Why the Note Was Written
sections.content:
The authors, E. Harslem and J. Heafner of RAND, issued this note because of recent discussions of protocols and data formats. It first covers some specific sequences, then offers thoughts on two general implementation approaches.

The authors say they want the emphasis on the general solutions, not on the specifics.
sections.plainLanguage: Some people were arguing about how computers should greet each other. The authors wrote down what they thought, and said the big idea matters more than the small details.

sections.title: The Initial Connection Protocol, Restated
sections.content:
The note makes two points about an Initial Connection Protocol (ICP). First, it restates the ICP of RFC 66. The authors see one technical error: as diagrammed, both server and user send all messages before the connections are established, which is inconsistent with Network Document No. 1. They also say a standard ICP should apply to more than a process calling a logger, so the process name field of the server socket should be a parameter, with zero as the special case for loggers.

In the restatement, the user sends RTS, the server answers with STR (or refuses by closing), the user allocates space with ALL, and the server sends an even 32 bit number over the connection. That number is the server's receive socket; it and the next higher socket are reserved for the user. The server then sends CLS, and both sides exchange STR and RTS messages for the duplex connection.

Second, the note proposes a variant. Steps 3 and 4 are deleted, and the user listens on sockets US and US + 1 for calls from the server. The authors say this reduces the number of network messages by two and passes the server's socket information only once.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people want a private phone line. The old way has them swap the number first and then call. The new way skips the swap: one person just waits by two phones and the other calls them.

sections.title: Adapting to Data Formats: The Form Machine
sections.content:
The authors want to adopt the data format suggestions in RFC 42 and RFC 63, and they subscribe to multiple standards for particular problem classes. They also want to bring in programs not planned with the network in mind, and they say requiring extensive front-ends on each such program is not a reasonable goal.

Their answer is the Form Machine, an experimental package of the finite state machine class that recognizes a form of regular expressions describing data formats. They picture Form Machines at service providing hosts to reduce network traffic. The current version offers character code translation (decimal, octal, hexadecimal, 8 bit ASCII, 7 bit ASCII, EBCDIC and binary), multiple break strings, literal insertion, skipping strings, record sequence numbers, string-length insertion, arbitrary string lengths, concatenation of network messages and field transposition.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a translator sitting between two people who speak different languages. The Form Machine is that translator for the shapes of data, so nobody has to rebuild their whole program.

sections.title: Adapting to Command Sequences: The Protocol Manager
sections.content:
RAND's Network Services Program lets terminal users and programs work at the NCP level, issuing commands such as LISTEN and INIT. That hands-on approach suits exploration, but it makes a researcher repeat the same handshaking again and again.

The Protocol Manager, a planned module of that program, would let a user define, store, retrieve and execute canned protocol sequences. Sequences may contain break points where the console user injects information, and command parameters may contain tokens filled in by the remote party. The example given is the socket number the server supplies in RFC 66, which the user reuses in later RTS and STR commands.

The note ends by asking readers whether adaptation to data formats and protocol is a reasonable approach and what it should cover.
sections.plainLanguage: If you call the same friend every day, you can save the whole dialing routine on a button. The Protocol Manager saves a computer's long hello routine so you press one button instead.
